claims: the states a transaction can occupy between creation and a final outcome, such as signed but not yet submitted, pending at one or more nodes, included in a block, and final, and why before inclusion its status is not one shared fact: the sender, each node and the chain can hold different views of it, so a transaction unknown to one node may be pending at another and be included by a producer the sender never reached. Mempools, Transaction Propagation and Transaction Inclusion are named, not explained

the returns that make the lifecycle a state model rather than a forward pipeline: a pending transaction can be dropped by nodes, for example evicted or no longer relayed, without becoming invalid, and can become pending again if anyone still holding it resubmits it and a node admits it; it can be replaced by a conflicting transaction from the same sender, one that uses the same sequence number or spends the same input, so that at most one of them can be included; and an included transaction whose block is removed by a reorganization before it is final can return to pending, be included again in another block, or become invalid if a conflicting transaction took its place. Reorganizations and the finality concepts are named, not explained

the outcomes a transaction can end in and how its sender tells them apart: included and executed successfully, included but reverted, or never included because a conflicting transaction consumed its sequence number or input or, where the format provides one, its expiry passed; why without such an end a dropped transaction is not retired, and anyone holding a copy can submit it later, so a sender that wants to cancel a pending transaction generally has to get a conflicting one included; and why, in account-based designs with sequence numbers, tracking a transaction by its identifier can lose sight of it when a replacement with a different identifier is the one included, while the sender and sequence number identify the slot the competing versions contend for

what each group of a transaction's fields is for: authorization (a signature, with the sender either carried explicitly or recovered from the signature), the requested action (a target, a value and input data, or initialization code when the transaction creates a contract), fee terms (a limit on the metered resources it may consume and the price, or maximum price, the sender will pay per unit) and validity scope (in many account-based formats a sequence number and a chain identifier, and in some formats an expiry or a reference to a recent block); and why the signature has to cover every field that can change the transaction's effect or cost, since a field outside the signed content can be altered by whoever relays the transaction, unless the format lets the signer deliberately leave some open to others. Replay Protection, Account Nonces and Transaction Data are named, not explained

how a format can separate roles that a simple transaction gives to one party: the account that authorizes the action, the account whose state the action acts from, and the account that pays the fee; what a format must carry when these differ, such as several required signatures with one of them designated as fee payer, a sponsor's separate authorization, or data an account's own code interprets as authorization instead of a fixed signature field; Account Abstraction is named, not explained

why many transaction formats are typed: a type identifier ahead of the encoded fields lets a protocol add fields, such as new fee terms, declarations of the state a transaction will access, or references to attached data, without making existing encodings ambiguous, keeps older formats decodable under their original rules, and, when the type is part of the signed content, keeps a signature made for one format from being accepted for another; and what it costs: every validating node must support every type still accepted, so adding a type is a protocol change. Blob Transactions is named, not explained

why many designs compute a transaction's identifier from its encoding, and what malleability does to it: if the encoding or the signature admits more than one valid form for the same authorized contents, the same transaction can circulate under several identifiers, misleading anything that tracks it by identifier; and the counters designs use, such as a single canonical encoding, accepting only one form of each signature, or computing the identifier over content that excludes the signature. Digital Signatures and Signature Verification are named, not explained

the difference between state-independent checks, such as well-formed encoding, field ranges, a signature that verifies over the contents against the key it names or the sender recovered from it and a matching chain identifier, whose result under the same protocol rules does not depend on state and so holds wherever the transaction is evaluated, and state-dependent checks, such as a sequence number matching the account's next one, a balance covering the largest fee the transaction can incur, and a fee bid meeting the current minimum price, whose result holds only against the state they were checked against; and why this split decides what a node can check once and reuse, and what has to be evaluated again against the pre-state at the transaction's position

where validity as a protocol rule ends and admission policy begins: a validity rule is applied identically by every validator to a transaction at its position, while each node's admission policy, such as a minimum fee or a limit on pending transactions per sender, decides only what that node holds and relays, may be stricter than validity and may differ between nodes, so a transaction one node refused can still be validly included; and what happens to an ordered transaction that fails a validity rule: in designs that validate blocks by executing them, the block containing it is invalid, while designs that order transactions without executing them, such as some rollups, have every node skip it by the same rule. Transaction Admission, Mempool Policies and Block Validation are named, not explained

where a protocol draws the line between validity and successful execution, and why: validity is decided before anyone has paid, so a design keeps it to conditions that are cheap and bounded to decide, while conditions that need arbitrary computation, such as what a contract requires of its inputs, are checked during execution, where a failure is charged to the sender as a reverted transaction rather than borne by the nodes that rejected it; Transaction Reversion owns what the reverted outcome records and keeps

how validation cost is bounded where anyone can submit transactions: since rejecting an invalid transaction is unpaid work, many designs keep each check bounded, such as a fixed set of signature schemes and a few state lookups, and where validity is decided by an account's own code, they restrict that code, such as limiting its computation and the state it may read, so that validating stays cheap and a single state change can invalidate only a bounded number of pending transactions after nodes have spent work admitting them; Account Abstraction and Denial-of-Service Resistance are named, not explained

the protocol steps around the code a transaction triggers and why they come in that order, as in many account-based designs with metered execution, such as Ethereum: before the payload runs, the protocol charges or reserves the fee for the transaction's full declared resource limit and advances the sender's sequence number, outside what a failure of the payload can undo, while other designs only check the sender's sequence number and fee coverage beforehand and apply the charge and the sequence-number update in a closing step that a payload failure does not undo; it then runs the payload, a value transfer, a call into code or a contract creation, under that limit; and afterwards, in designs that charge by usage, such as Ethereum, it settles, refunding the unused part of the charge and distributing the fee as the protocol directs, such as to the block producer or by burning part of it, so that the final charge reflects the resources actually used. Gas, Fees, Fee Accounting and Account Nonces are named, not explained; why a reverted transaction keeps the charge and the sequence-number update is Transaction Reversion's

what executing one transaction produces: the post-state, which becomes the pre-state of the next transaction in the block, and a per-transaction record of the outcome, such as a success or failure status, the resources consumed and the logs emitted, which many designs gather into receipts; and why the record is needed beside the post-state, since in designs that include failed transactions a failed one changes no state beyond its fee charge, its sequence-number update and any other effects the protocol applies outside the payload, yet its inclusion and failure must stay observable to its sender and to anyone reading the chain. Logs, Events and State Roots are named, not explained; committing results so that nodes detect divergence is Deterministic Execution's

why transaction execution is a different unit from running code: one transaction may run no code at all, as a plain transfer, the code of many contracts through nested calls, or the initialization code a creation runs to produce the code it installs, while the protocol's envelope of charging, sequence-number update, settlement and outcome record applies once per transaction whatever runs inside it; Contract Execution owns one invocation of a contract's code and Execution Context what that code can read

what the all-or-nothing unit covers inside one transaction: the state changes made by every call it makes, nested to any depth, including value transfers, storage writes, contracts created and, in designs such as the EVM, emitted logs; and what designs that keep a failed transaction's fee and sequence-number update place outside the unit, so that it is narrower than everything the transaction's processing changes. Why those survive a failure is Transaction Reversion's

how execution environments provide the unit on one state machine: recording each change in a journal so that it can be undone on failure, or buffering changes in a working copy that is applied only on success; the trade-off between them, such as cheap reads against the live state versus cheap discards; and why designs that let a caller continue after a callee fails need nested checkpoints, one per call, while designs in which any failure aborts the transaction need only one, so that a failure can be undone back to the point where the failing call began

where the unit is narrowed: in designs that let a caller handle a callee's failure, such as the EVM, a caller that handles it instead of propagating it keeps its own changes while the callee's are undone, so all-or-nothing holds per call, and the transaction as a whole is all-or-nothing only along paths where failures propagate; and why a successful status therefore does not show that every action the transaction attempted took effect. Contract Calls and Unchecked External Calls are named, not explained

what atomicity does not provide and where its scope ends: it does not hide a transaction's intermediate states from code the transaction itself calls, which can observe and act on them before the transaction finishes, so all-or-nothing is not isolation within a transaction; and it covers one transaction on one state machine, while all-or-nothing across several transactions, as with bundles, or across chains is provided, where it is, by other mechanisms. Reentrancy, Bundle Atomicity and Atomicity Guarantees are named, not explained

what triggers a revert and how the triggers differ in what the failure costs: an explicit revert by the running code, a failed check, running out of metered resources, or an invalid operation; and why, in the EVM for example, an explicit revert returns the unused part of the failing call's resource allowance while an exceptional halt consumes all of it, so the trigger decides how much of the failing call's allowance, and so of the sender's fee, a failure consumes. Gas and Metering are named, not explained

what reversion undoes and what survives it in designs that include failed transactions: state changes and emitted logs are discarded, while the fee charged for the attempt, the sequence-number update, in designs that use sequence numbers, and a record of the failure remain; and why each survives: an uncharged failure would let a sender impose execution work on every node at no cost, a sequence number left unspent would let the same signed transaction be executed again, and the record lets the sender and others see that it was included and failed

how a failure is reported and used: revert data returned to the caller, such as an error identifier with arguments, which a calling contract can decode, handle or pass upward, while in some designs, such as the EVM's receipts, it is not kept in the transaction's record, so an outside observer recovers the reason by re-executing the transaction; and reverting as an enforcement tool, code that checks a condition such as an access right or a minimum acceptable result and reverts when it fails, so effects that depended on it never land where the failure propagates, at the price of the fee for the attempt and with protection only for the conditions the code checks

the difference between an invalid transaction and a reverted one in their consequences: in designs that validate blocks by executing them, an invalid transaction cannot be included, so it leaves no record, costs its sender nothing and leaves its sequence number free, while a reverted one is included, recorded as failed, charged and consumes its sequence number; and why designs that make every condition a validity rule, as Bitcoin does with its scripts, have no reverted outcome at all, since a failing condition makes the transaction invalid. Transaction Validation owns where the line between the two is drawn

sequence: Typical forward path: signed (held by sender, no node) -> submitted to one or more nodes -> pending (held by at least one node, possibly relayed onward; possibly held only by a producer or builder reached directly) -> included in a block -> block becomes final.
The forward path is the special case, not the model: dropping, replacement and reorganization send the transaction back or end it without inclusion.
Ordering within a block (position) is transaction-ordering's; validation and execution steps are siblings'. Name them, do not walk through them.
actors: Sender: signs, keeps a copy, may resubmit, may sign a conflicting transaction for the same slot (replacement or cancellation).
Nodes: each holds and relays by its own admission policy (named, not explained), may evict or stop relaying; each has only its own view.
Block producer: includes what it holds; can include a transaction the sender never sent to it, reached through relay.
Anyone holding a copy: once broadcast, copies are not under the sender's control; any holder can resubmit later.
Trackers (wallets, explorers): observe partial views; see failures field on identifier-based tracking.
assumptions: Status before inclusion is per-observer: the sender's, each node's, and the chain's views can differ. 'Pending' in the model means held by at least one node; no single participant can observe that no node holds it.

Do not imply inclusion makes status one shared fact either: before finality, nodes following different branches can disagree about inclusion. The claim only says the pre-inclusion status is not shared; do not overstate the converse.

Reorganization returns arise in designs where an included block can be removed before an observer counts it final. In designs whose blocks are final when committed (many BFT-style protocols), included is final, and a committed block is removed only if the protocol's safety assumptions fail. State the condition; do not say every chain reorganizes.

Under probabilistic finality, 'final' is a confidence threshold the observer chooses (depth), not an absolute state: a reorganization deeper than that threshold is unlikely but not impossible. So Final (and Never includable, which rests on a competitor being final or on the expiry passing in a final block) holds to the observer's threshold, or under deterministic finality to the protocol's safety assumptions. Name probabilistic and deterministic finality, do not explain them.

Conflicts: account-based designs with sequence numbers (same sender, same sequence number) and UTXO designs (same input spent). 'At most one can be included' holds within any one chain history; across a reorganization the competitor on the surviving branch is the one that counts.

Resubmitting a dropped transaction makes it pending again only where a node admits it: admission policy can refuse it again (for example, the low fee that got it evicted). Keep that condition; do not say resubmission always succeeds.

'Without an end a dropped transaction stays valid': hold as 'is not retired / stays includable'. In account-based designs its state-dependent checks (such as a balance covering the fee) can fail for a time and pass again later; what never lapses on its own is the authorization, unless an expiry field exists. Do not claim it is valid at every moment.
Expiry exists only where the format provides one (a deadline block height or time, or a reference to a recent block that ages out). Many formats have none.
failures: Treating eviction or disappearance from one node's view as cancellation: the transaction can resurface and be included later, possibly in a changed state where its effect differs.
Treating included-but-not-final as final in designs with reorganizations.

Tracking by identifier: in account-based designs a replacement for the same sender and sequence number has a different identifier; if the replacement is included, the original's identifier never appears on chain and an identifier-based tracker sees 'still pending' or 'lost'. Track the slot (sender + sequence number; in UTXO designs, the spent input). Identifier malleability is transaction-structure's: different cause, do not explain it here.
Reading 'included' as 'succeeded': included-but-reverted is an included outcome; why it is charged and what it keeps is transaction-reversion's.
states: Held by no node: signed, valid for inclusion, but no node holds it. Covers both not-yet-submitted and dropped; the point is that the two are the same situation (any holder can submit it).
Pending: held by at least one node or producer, not in a block on the chain the observer follows.
Included: in a block that is not yet final (only where blocks can be removed before finality).

Final: in a final block, as far as the finality it rests on holds (the observer's depth threshold, or the protocol's safety assumptions). Outcome is either executed successfully or reverted; the sender tells them apart from the recorded outcome status (record contents are transaction-execution's; reverted consequences are transaction-reversion's).

Never includable: a conflicting transaction for the same slot is final, or the format's expiry has passed in a block that is final. The sender tells this apart by seeing the slot consumed by another transaction (sequence number advanced / input spent) or the expiry passed in a final block, not by the transaction's own identifier.
transitions: Held by no node -> Pending: submitted, or resubmitted by anyone holding a copy, and admitted by some node.
Pending -> Held by no node: every node and producer that held it evicts or discards it; it does not become invalid. A node that stops relaying it still holds it.
Pending -> Included: a producer includes it in a block.

Included -> Pending: a reorganization removes its block before it is final and the surviving branch does not also include it; nodes that take it back hold it as pending, and it can be included again in another block. A transaction the surviving branch also includes stays included, in another block.
Included -> Final: its block becomes final.
Held by no node -> Never includable, and Pending -> Never includable: a conflicting transaction for the same slot becomes final, or expiry passes in a block that is final.
Included -> Never includable: a reorganization removes its block and a conflicting transaction takes its place on the surviving branch, and that becomes final.

Condition the move to Never includable on finality, of the conflicting transaction or of a block in which the expiry has passed: before that, a conflicting transaction included in a non-final block can itself be reorganized out, and an expiry passed on a branch a reorganization later replaces does not bind the surviving branch.
invariants: Of transactions competing for one slot (same sender and sequence number, or same input), at most one is included in any one chain history.

Nothing but a conflicting inclusion or an expiry retires a signed transaction; eviction, non-relay and the sender's wish do not. Hence cancelling generally means getting a conflicting transaction (such as a zero-value transfer to oneself with the same sequence number) included first; it is a race, not a guaranteed cancel.
variants: Account-based with sequence numbers: the slot is (sender, sequence number); replacement and cancellation reuse the sequence number; identifier tracking can lose a replaced transaction.
UTXO: the slot is the spent input(s); a conflicting spend of the same input excludes the other.
Formats with expiry: an end without any conflicting transaction. Formats without: no such end.
Designs with immediate finality: no Included-but-not-final state, no reorganization returns.
Do not develop these into a comparison: they condition the claims, one sentence each where needed.

design.relationship: A transaction's persistent states (held by no node, pending, included, final, never includable) and the events or conditions that move it between them, including returns from pending to held by no node and from included to pending, with two different end states.

structures.purpose: Show the five states in the order a transaction usually moves through them, each transition with its condition (submitted or resubmitted; evicted or no longer relayed; included; block removed by a reorganization before finality; block final; conflicting transaction final or expiry passed), the two returns, and the two final states (final with success or revert, never includable).
structures.whyNotProse: The claims' point is that the lifecycle is not the forward pipeline the domain flow suggests: states can be left backward, dropped and unsubmitted are the same state, and there are two different kinds of end. In prose the returns read as exceptions to a pipeline spread over several sentences; a state model shows at once which states can be left backward, under which condition, and which states are final.

design.division: The state model shows the states, each transition's condition, the returns and which states are final; the prose must not walk through the transitions again. The prose explains what the model cannot: that status before inclusion is a per-observer view (the model's states are the transaction's situation across the network and chain, which no single party observes); why dropping does not invalidate and why a dropped and an unsubmitted transaction are equivalent; replacement and the at-most-one invariant per slot; the condition that reorganization returns exist only where inclusion can be reversed before finality; how the sender tells success, revert and never-included apart; why cancelling means getting a conflicting transaction included; and why tracking by slot rather than identifier.
design.level: Belongs here, not at Transactions (which defines the unit and its boundaries, not its course over time), and not at mempools, inclusion, reorganizations or finality, each of which owns the mechanism behind one transition; this concept owns how those transitions compose into one transaction's states and ends.
design.territory: The transitions name eviction, relay, inclusion, reorganization, finality and expiry as conditions without explaining their mechanisms (mempools, mempool-policies, transaction-admission, transaction-propagation, transaction-inclusion, reorganizations and the finality concepts stay excluded). Position within a block is not drawn (transaction-ordering, name only). Success and revert share one final state; what a revert keeps and costs is transaction-reversion's, the outcome record's contents transaction-execution's, validity checks transaction-validation's, identifier malleability transaction-structure's. The model does not restate the domain flow's Structure, Validation, Ordering, Execution stages.

audit.note: Re-audit after repair cycle 2, scoped to findings/transaction-lifecycle-2.md R1 (expiry-based Never includable end not conditioned on finality); earlier findings (transaction-lifecycle.md, -b.md) were confirmed resolved by the previous re-audit. R1 resolved: the P4 summary now reads 'the final state and the never-includable end, whether that end rests on a competing transaction being final or on an expiry passing in a block that is final, hold only as far as the observer's threshold or the protocol's safety assumptions hold'; both expiry transitions in the state block (Held by no node -> Never includable, Pending -> Never includable) now say 'the format's expiry passes in a block that is final'; P5 ('seeing it pass in a block that is final') and P6 ('wait for it to pass in a block that is final') match; the model's transitions, assumptions and states fields carry the same condition, and the transitions note explains why (an expiry passed on a branch a reorganization later replaces does not bind the surviving branch). Re-read every other use of 'expiry', 'final' and 'never includable' (definition, state block, P4, P5, P6) for consistency: no contradiction between the summary and the conditioned sentences. (2) Model invariants 'Nothing but a conflicting inclusion or an expiry retires a signed transaction' is not conditioned on finality as the record now is. (3) Carried over from the previous re-audit: P1 'public record' unscoped for permissioned chains; P5 'no trace under the transaction's own identifier' (say 'on the chain'); no Pending -> Final edge where committed blocks are final (carried in prose, accepted by design); 'without it becoming invalid' (not permanently invalid); P7 identifier-tracking loss limited to account-based designs; P4 'unlikely' could name the protocol's assumptions.

contents: Four groups, scoped: the grouping as listed fits account-based formats (Ethereum-style); state the scope. UTXO formats differ: no sender or target account, authorization is per spent output (a script or witness satisfying it). In Bitcoin the fee is implicit (inputs minus outputs) and there is no limit on metered resources; other UTXO designs (e.g. Cardano) carry an explicit fee and per-script execution budgets, so scope those two statements to Bitcoin. Mention the difference only as far as needed to keep the general statements true.
Authorization: signature(s); sender carried explicitly (e.g. Solana lists signer keys) or recovered from the signature (Ethereum ECDSA). Not how signatures work (Digital Signatures named).

Requested action: in Ethereum-style formats one target, a value and input data; contract creation as an empty target plus initialization code is an EVM-style convention, say 'in designs such as the EVM'. Some formats (e.g. Solana) carry a list of instructions, each naming a program and the accounts it touches, so 'a target' is not universal. The input data's contents and encoding are Transaction Data's/Calldata's: name only.

Fee terms: a limit on metered resources and a price or maximum price per unit (EIP-1559 carries maximum fee and maximum priority fee per unit). State what the fields bound; do not explain how fees are computed, charged or refunded (Fees, Gas, Transaction Execution).

Validity scope: in many account-based formats a sequence number and a chain identifier; some carry an expiry (e.g. a timeout height or expiration time) or a recent-block reference that also bounds lifetime (Solana's recent blockhash). Not every format has a sequence number or a chain identifier: Solana uses a recent blockhash; Bitcoin has neither (an output can be spent only once). Name Replay Protection and Account Nonces; do not explain how they prevent replay (parent already says why they exist).

Pitfall: 'signed content' is not the same as 'transmitted fields': some formats sign values the verifier supplies rather than carries, e.g. the chain identifier in Cosmos' sign document, or in EIP-155 legacy signing where it is folded into the signing hash and the v value.
fields.producedBy: The sender's wallet or client assembles the fields and signs; with separated roles, several parties sign or authorize. How a transaction is assembled, estimated and signed is Transaction Construction's: name only.
fields.checkedBy: Validating nodes decode it under its type's rules and check its authorization and fields; what is checked when, stateless vs state-dependent, is Transaction Validation's and Signature Verification's. Name only; say the structure is what those checks read.
proves: A valid signature shows that the holder of the key authorized exactly the signed content, assuming the key is not compromised. It says nothing about fields outside the signed content: whoever relays the transaction (a node, a relayer, a bundler) can alter those, so a field that changes the effect or the cost (target, value, input data, fee limit or price, chain identifier, type) must be inside it, or a relayer could, for example, raise the fee price or redirect the value.

Condition the 'must cover' claim: some formats let the signer deliberately leave parts open, e.g. Bitcoin's signature-hash modes (ANYONECANPAY lets others add inputs; NONE leaves outputs unsigned). Then the signer accepts that others can change them. Do not say every format signs every field.

The signature cannot cover itself, and in many designs other witness data sits outside the signed content: that is where malleability enters (claim 4), changing the identifier but not the authorized effect.
fields.lifetime: Only as the validity-scope fields bound it: a signed transaction stays usable until what those fields refer to is used up or passes (its sequence number consumed, the expiry or the referenced recent block too old). The states and outcomes a transaction passes through are Transaction Lifecycle's: do not describe them.
variants: Role separation (claim 2). Simple account-based transaction: one party authorizes, is acted from and pays. Formats that separate them must carry an authorization from each party whose account is debited or acted from. Examples, each scoped: Solana carries several signatures over one message, the first signer paying the fee; Aptos-style sponsored transactions carry a separate fee-payer signature; Cosmos fee grants let a granter pay under an authorization it recorded beforehand, rather than a signature in the transaction; account-code authorization (e.g. Starknet accounts, ERC-4337 user operations) puts data the account's own code checks in place of a fixed signature field.

Distinguish protocol-level separation (the format carries the roles) from separation built above a simple format (meta-transactions, ERC-4337): there the outer transaction is ordinary and signed and paid by a relayer or bundler, and the user's authorization travels as data a contract checks. Do not explain Account Abstraction's machinery (entry point, bundlers, paymaster validation): name it.

Pitfall: a fee payer that is not the authorizer must authorize the fee debit by some means (signature, prior grant, or its own code accepting it); otherwise anyone could make it pay. Say 'must authorize the debit', not 'must sign'.

Typed formats (claim 3), example EIP-2718: a type byte ahead of the payload; legacy encodings begin with a byte no type uses, so decoding is unambiguous; types added access lists (state the transaction declares it will access, type 1), new fee terms (type 2), blob references (type 3), authorization lists (type 4). Scope: 'many formats', not all; others version or extend formats differently (Bitcoin's version field and SegWit's marker; Cosmos' typed messages inside a transaction). Do not number Ethereum's types in the record unless needed; do not explain Blob Transactions.
invariants: Every field that can change the effect or cost is inside the signed content, unless the format deliberately lets the signer leave it open.

When the type is part of the signed content (as in EIP-2718 types, which hash the type byte with the payload), a signature for one format cannot be reinterpreted as a valid signature for another, because the signed bytes differ. Condition it on the type being signed.
Identifier vs authorized contents: an identifier is stable only if each authorized content has one valid encoding and one valid signature form, or if the identifier excludes what can vary.
tradeoffs: Typing: extensibility without ambiguity vs every validating node must decode and validate every type still accepted, so a new type is a protocol change (a hard fork in Ethereum) and old types persist while accepted. Wallets and tooling must also support them, but keep the claim's cost to the validating side.

Role separation: sponsored or multi-party transactions vs more signatures to verify, a payer exposed to paying for others' failures, and, where account code authorizes, unbounded validation that validators must restrict (that restriction is Transaction Validation's: name only).
relation: Identifier (claim 4): Ethereum's transaction hash is the hash of the full signed encoding (type byte plus payload); Bitcoin's txid is the double SHA-256 of the serialization without witness data, while the wtxid covers it; Solana identifies a transaction by its first signature. So 'computed from its encoding' holds for many designs, not all: scope it.

Malleability: more than one valid encoding of the same fields (non-canonical length or integer encodings), more than one valid signature form for the same contents (ECDSA: (r, s) and (r, n - s) both verify), or unlocking data outside the signed content that its condition accepts in more than one form (e.g. data a script ignores) gives one authorized transaction several identifiers. Harm: wallets, exchanges and services tracking by identifier can report a payment missing or retry it; in UTXO designs such as Bitcoin's, later transactions reference outputs by txid, so a malleated parent invalidates pre-signed children (a reason Bitcoin's SegWit moved witness data out of the txid).

Counters and their limits: canonical encoding (Ethereum requires canonical RLP; Bitcoin's BIP 66 strict DER) and one signature form (Ethereum's low-s rule since Homestead; in Bitcoin low-s is relay policy, not consensus, so it reduces rather than eliminates malleation) stop third parties re-encoding an existing transaction's fields or deriving a second form of its signature; they do not fix what other unlocking data contains where its condition accepts data the check ignores (rules on that data's form narrow this but cannot cover every condition), and they do not stop the signer producing a second valid signature with a fresh nonce. Excluding the signature and other unlocking data from the identifier (SegWit txid) removes their variation from the identifier for both, but not changes to signed fields.

Boundary with Transaction Lifecycle: malleability is the same authorized content under several identifiers; a replacement is different content contending for the same sequence number, which is Lifecycle's. Do not explain replacement; at most contrast in a clause.

model.meaning: Transaction validation is the evaluation of a transaction against the protocol's validity rules, the conditions it must meet to be includable at its position, which decides whether it may be processed at all, as distinct from whether its execution succeeds.

parents.transactions: Premise, not to re-teach: validity is judged more than once and can change between admission and execution because earlier transactions spend funds or use the sequence number. Adds: which checks depend on state and which do not, and so what is reused vs re-evaluated at the position; protocol validity vs a node's admission policy; what an ordered invalid transaction does to a block (execute-to-validate) or how it is skipped (order-without-execute); where designs draw the validity/execution line and why (cost before payment); how validation cost is bounded, including when an account's own code decides validity. Do not restate that one authorization is single-use and chain-bound (parent; Transaction Structure, Replay Protection).

claims: the difference between state-independent checks, such as well-formed encoding, field ranges, a signature that verifies over the contents against the key it names or the sender recovered from it and a matching chain identifier, whose result under the same protocol rules does not depend on state and so holds wherever the transaction is evaluated, and state-dependent checks, such as a sequence number matching the account's next one, a balance covering the largest fee the transaction can incur, and a fee bid meeting the current minimum price, whose result holds only against the state they were checked against; and why this split decides what a node can check once and reuse, and what has to be evaluated again against the pre-state at the transaction's position

where validity as a protocol rule ends and admission policy begins: a validity rule is applied identically by every validator to a transaction at its position, while each node's admission policy, such as a minimum fee or a limit on pending transactions per sender, decides only what that node holds and relays, may be stricter than validity and may differ between nodes, so a transaction one node refused can still be validly included; and what happens to an ordered transaction that fails a validity rule: in designs that validate blocks by executing them, the block containing it is invalid, while designs that order transactions without executing them, such as some rollups, have every node skip it by the same rule. Transaction Admission, Mempool Policies and Block Validation are named, not explained

where a protocol draws the line between validity and successful execution, and why: validity is decided before anyone has paid, so a design keeps it to conditions that are cheap and bounded to decide, while conditions that need arbitrary computation, such as what a contract requires of its inputs, are checked during execution, where a failure is charged to the sender as a reverted transaction rather than borne by the nodes that rejected it; Transaction Reversion owns what the reverted outcome records and keeps

how validation cost is bounded where anyone can submit transactions: since rejecting an invalid transaction is unpaid work, many designs keep each check bounded, such as a fixed set of signature schemes and a few state lookups, and where validity is decided by an account's own code, they restrict that code, such as limiting its computation and the state it may read, so that validating stays cheap and a single state change can invalidate only a bounded number of pending transactions after nodes have spent work admitting them; Account Abstraction and Denial-of-Service Resistance are named, not explained

placements.transaction-validation: Single placement, under Transactions in Computation & Execution. Still write it so it stands without the parent: state the premise it starts from in a clause at most (validity is evaluated at more than one point), then go beyond it.

inputs: the transaction's bytes and the protocol rules in force (fork/version): enough for state-independent checks

state-dependent checks add the pre-state at the evaluation point: for a node at admission, its view of the head state; for a producer or validator, the pre-state at the transaction's position, which includes earlier transactions in the same block (the same sender's among them)

context of the including block for checks such as an expiry against height or time, a reference to a recent block, or a block-level minimum fee: these depend on where it lands, not on contents alone, so treat them with the position-dependent checks for reuse
outputs: a verdict relative to a rule set and, for state-dependent checks, to one state: valid here, or invalid with the failed rule

a state-independent result can be cached with the exact transaction and rule set and reused across admission, relay, block building and block validation; a state-dependent result is a snapshot that a new head or an earlier transaction at the position can overturn, in either direction (a balance can be topped up, a sequence-number gap filled)
actors: nodes applying admission policy to what they hold and relay (policy: theirs, may differ, may be stricter than validity; Transaction Admission and Mempool Policies named only)
block producers, who must only include valid transactions where an invalid one invalidates the block
validators/full nodes applying the same validity rules at the position; 'identically' holds for nodes following the protocol (a node applying different rules diverges from the others)
in some designs, the account's own code, which decides part of validity
assumptions: the validity/execution line argument assumes designs with metered execution that include failed transactions and charge for them (account-based, EVM-like). Bitcoin-style designs make every spending condition a validity rule and keep it bounded instead (script size and signature-operation limits, no unbounded loops); Reversion names Bitcoin for 'no reverted outcome': do not explain that outcome here

the reason for the line: validity is decided before any fee is charged, so it is kept to conditions cheap and bounded to decide; among them the conditions that establish the transaction is authorized and can pay the most it can consume (e.g. balance covering the maximum fee and the value), so whatever execution follows is paid for; conditions needing arbitrary computation are left to execution, where failure is charged to the sender
'state-independent' holds only under the same protocol rules: a fork that changes rules (types, schemes, chain identifier) requires re-evaluation
cost bounding is 'many designs', not universal
failures: an ordered transaction failing a validity rule: in designs that validate blocks by executing them, the block is invalid; in designs that order without executing, such as some rollups, every node skips it by the same deterministic rule. Do not name a specific rollup unless sure of its rule; Block Validation named only

unbounded or state-sensitive validation enables unpaid-work abuse: transactions that are expensive to reject, or many pending transactions invalidated by one state change after nodes spent work admitting them (Denial-of-Service Resistance named only)
a node refusing a transaction under its policy is not evidence the transaction is invalid; it can still be validly included by a producer that received it elsewhere
variants: state-independent checks: encoding well formed, field ranges, signature valid over the contents, chain identifier matching. Pitfall: signature validity is state-independent only as cryptographic verification against a key that the transaction carries or from which the sender is recovered. Where an account's keys are kept in state and can be changed, or the account's code decides authorization, whether the signature authorizes the account is state-dependent. In UTXO designs verification needs the spent output's locking data; outputs do not change, so that result can be reused, but whether the output is still unspent is state-dependent

state-dependent checks: sequence number equal to the account's next, balance covering the largest fee it can incur (and value where the design requires it), fee bid at or above the current minimum price
conditions decided during execution: anything requiring arbitrary computation, such as what a contract requires of its inputs (not validity in metered designs)
tradeoffs: expressiveness of validity vs cost of deciding it: richer validity (account code deciding authorization) lets accounts choose schemes but needs restrictions to stay cheap and stable

account-code validation restrictions (example: the rules ERC-4337 bundlers apply, ERC-7562): a computation limit, no reading of values that differ between validation and inclusion such as block time or number, and storage access limited to state associated with the account, with exceptions for staked entities throttled by reputation. Effect: one state change invalidates only a bounded set of pending transactions (those whose account's state changed, capped by per-sender limits), not 'none' and not 'cannot'; native account abstraction proposals impose similar limits. Give no specific numbers; Account Abstraction named only
a fixed set of signature schemes and a few state lookups keep each check bounded, at the cost of flexibility
invariants: a validity rule yields the same verdict for the same transaction at the same position under the same rules at every node following the protocol; admission policy has no such requirement

where an invalid transaction cannot be included, no fee is charged for evaluating it, which is why rejection is unpaid work for the node; designs differ (some charge fees for certain failures detected before execution), so scope the statement. The consequences of invalid vs reverted (record, fee, sequence number) are Transaction Reversion's: name the outcome, do not describe what it records or keeps

claims: the protocol steps around the code a transaction triggers and why they come in that order, as in many account-based designs with metered execution, such as Ethereum: before the payload runs, the protocol charges or reserves the fee for the transaction's full declared resource limit and advances the sender's sequence number, outside what a failure of the payload can undo, while other designs only check the sender's sequence number and fee coverage beforehand and apply the charge and the sequence-number update in a closing step that a payload failure does not undo; it then runs the payload, a value transfer, a call into code or a contract creation, under that limit; and afterwards, in designs that charge by usage, such as Ethereum, it settles, refunding the unused part of the charge and distributing the fee as the protocol directs, such as to the block producer or by burning part of it, so that the final charge reflects the resources actually used. Gas, Fees, Fee Accounting and Account Nonces are named, not explained; why a reverted transaction keeps the charge and the sequence-number update is Transaction Reversion's

what executing one transaction produces: the post-state, which becomes the pre-state of the next transaction in the block, and a per-transaction record of the outcome, such as a success or failure status, the resources consumed and the logs emitted, which many designs gather into receipts; and why the record is needed beside the post-state, since in designs that include failed transactions a failed one changes no state beyond its fee charge, its sequence-number update and any other effects the protocol applies outside the payload, yet its inclusion and failure must stay observable to its sender and to anyone reading the chain. why transaction execution is a different unit from running code: one transaction may run no code at all, as a plain transfer, the code of many contracts through nested calls, or the initialization code a creation runs to produce the code it installs, while the protocol's envelope of charging, sequence-number update, settlement and outcome record applies once per transaction whatever runs inside it; Contract Execution owns one invocation of a contract's code and Execution Context what that code can read

sequence: Scope first: the envelope described is that of account-based designs with metered execution, per-account sequence numbers and inclusion of failed transactions; say so, and do not present it as how every chain processes transactions. Within that scope the order of the protocol's own steps differs between designs (next item).

In many such designs, such as Ethereum, up front, before any payload code: charge (or reserve) the fee for the full declared resource limit at the price the protocol settles at, and advance the sender's sequence number. Other designs in the scope only check the sender's sequence number and fee coverage beforehand and apply the charge and the sequence-number update in a closing step after the payload; one conditioned sentence, naming no system unless sure. Either way both sit outside the part a payload failure undoes. Ethereum detail if used: the debit for the gas limit is limit x effective price, not limit x the sender's maximum price; checking that the balance covers the maximum is Transaction Validation's, not a step here.

Why charging comes first, in the designs that charge up front: the worst-case charge is known from the declared limit, and securing it before code runs keeps the payload from spending the balance that must pay for its own execution. Do not present this order or its reason as necessary for every design in scope. Reason is about ordering, not about why the charge survives a failure (Transaction Reversion's).

Sequence-number update: say only that it is applied outside the undoable part (up front in designs such as Ethereum, in the closing step in others), so it holds whatever the payload does. Why it must survive a failure (replay) is Transaction Reversion's; how account nonces work is Account Nonces' (named).

Payload: one of a value transfer, a call into code, or a contract creation, run under the declared limit; running out of the limit stops it (Metering/Gas named, not explained). The value moved belongs to the payload and is undone with it on failure; do not lump it with the fee charge.

Settlement after the payload: in designs that charge by usage it needs usage, which is known only when the payload ends; that is the reason it comes last. Where the full limit was charged up front (Ethereum), it refunds the unused part of that charge and distributes the fee as the protocol directs (for example, in Ethereum since EIP-1559, the base-fee part of the charge for gas used is burned and the priority part goes to the block's fee recipient).

'Resources actually used' means used as the metering rules count them: the rules can consume the whole remaining allowance on some failures (Transaction Reversion's) and can reduce the charge by capped refunds (Ethereum caps storage-clearing refunds). Do not say the charge equals the computation performed. Not every metered design refunds: Monad, for example, charges by the gas limit; keep refund-on-settlement scoped to designs that settle on usage (see claim-accuracy note).
Outputs last: the post-state, and the per-transaction outcome record.
actors: Every executing node applies the same steps identically (that results must match across nodes is Deterministic Execution's; name only).
Sender: pays the charge, has its sequence number advanced. Fee recipient / block producer: receives the distributed part. Contracts whose code runs: act inside the payload only.
In designs that separate the fee payer from the sender (Transaction Structure's), the charge falls on the payer; do not assume sender = payer as a universal.
inputs: The transaction (its limit, price terms, sequence number, target, value, payload) and the pre-state: the post-state of the previous transaction in the block's order, or for the first, the state the block starts from (which can include block-level steps applied before transactions in some designs; do not claim it is simply the previous block's final state).
outputs: Post-state, which is the pre-state of the next transaction in the block's order. In designs that execute transactions in parallel, the result must still equal this sequential chaining (Parallel Execution named only, if at all). The last transaction's post-state need not be the block's final state where block-level steps follow (e.g. Ethereum withdrawals); do not claim it is.

Per-transaction outcome record, such as status, resources consumed and logs; many designs gather these into receipts (Execution Receipts, Logs, Events named only). Ethereum details if used: receipts carry cumulative gas used in the block, so one transaction's consumption is a difference; pre-Byzantium receipts carried an intermediate state root instead of a status. Keep the list as 'such as'.

Why the record is needed beside the post-state: in designs that include failed transactions, a failed one leaves almost no trace in state (its fee charge and sequence-number update, plus any other effects the protocol applies outside the payload), so state alone does not show that it was included and failed; the record keeps that observable to the sender and to anyone reading the chain. Committing to records or states (State Roots) and detecting divergence are named only.
assumptions: Account-based state with per-account sequence numbers, metered execution with a declared limit, and inclusion of failed transactions. Without these (e.g. UTXO designs where any failing condition makes a transaction invalid), the envelope and the failed-transaction record do not apply as described; say so as scope, do not explain those designs.

The transaction already passed validity at its position (Transaction Validation's); execution here starts from a valid, included transaction. An invalid one is not executed into the block at all; do not describe that path.
failures: Payload failure: the payload's effects are undone and the envelope still runs (charge stands, sequence number stays advanced, settlement and record happen). Name Transaction Reversion and Transaction Atomicity for what is undone and why the rest survives; do not explain either.

Up-front steps are not all-inclusive: some designs apply further effects before the payload that a payload failure also does not undo (Ethereum's EIP-7702 authorizations, for example). Avoid wording that makes charge + sequence number the only state a failed transaction changes.
invariants: The envelope (charge, sequence-number update, settlement, outcome record) applies once per transaction, whatever and however much code runs inside, including none.
In designs that charge the full limit up front and settle on usage, the final charge never exceeds the up-front charge; the refund is what makes them differ.
Nonce increments that happen inside the payload (e.g. a contract's nonce when it creates another contract) are payload effects, not the envelope's sequence-number update; do not conflate.
variants: Payload kinds: plain value transfer to an account with no code (runs no code; a transfer to an account that has code, or delegates to code, runs that code); a call into code, which may nest calls into many contracts (Contract Calls, Message Calls named); a contract creation, which runs initialization code whose output becomes the installed code. The installed code is not what the creation runs (see claim-accuracy note).

Unit distinction: Contract Execution owns one invocation of a contract's code (entry, what it draws on, how it ends); Execution Context owns what that code can read. This concept owns only the per-transaction envelope and outputs; name both, explain neither.

design.relationship: A process: fixed protocol steps in a meaningful order (charge and sequence-number update, then the payload, then settlement, then the outputs) bracketing a payload that takes one of three forms and converges back into the same settlement and record. The order is what the first claim asks about, and the convergence of very different payloads into one envelope is the third claim's point.

structures.purpose: A flow of the per-transaction envelope: up-front charge and sequence-number update, then a parallel set of the payload kinds (value transfer, call into code that may nest further calls, contract creation running initialization code), converging into settlement (refund of the unused part, fee distribution), then the outputs (post-state and outcome record). Shows the order and that every payload kind passes through the same steps before and after.
structures.whyNotProse: The prose must spend its sentences on why each step sits where it does and why the record is needed; the bracket shape, fixed steps before and after, a branching payload in between, converging again, is spatial and is what the reader needs to hold. In prose the convergence of three payload kinds into one settlement disperses across sentences, and the envelope-per-transaction point reads as an assertion rather than a shape.

design.division: The prose states the scope (account-based, metered designs), explains why charging precedes the payload and settlement follows it, what 'used' means under metering, what the post-state chain and the outcome record are and why the record is needed, and why the transaction is a different unit from a code invocation. The flow shows only the order and the branching-converging shape, with short stage labels; it must not carry reasons or conditions, and the prose must not re-list the stages as a sequence the flow already shows.
design.level: The envelope and per-transaction outputs exist only at the transaction unit. The parent (Transactions) states what a transaction is and why its three boundaries coincide, not how the protocol processes one; Contract Execution covers one code invocation, which sits inside the payload stage only. So the process belongs here.
design.territory: The flow names the payload kinds and settlement as stages without explaining calls, creation, metering, fees or nonces (Contract Calls, Message Calls, Contract Deployment, Gas, Metering, Fees, Fee Accounting, Account Nonces named only). It draws no failure branch: what is undone and what survives a failure belong to Transaction Atomicity and Transaction Reversion; the inclusion and lifecycle states are Transaction Lifecycle's; validity checks before execution are Transaction Validation's and appear in no stage. Divergence detection is Deterministic Execution's.
design.placements: One leaf placement under Transactions; the flow and prose are self-contained, scoped explicitly to account-based designs with metered execution, and reference no sibling's position.

audit.note: Re-audit (repair cycle 1), expanded into a complete audit because the repair changed the argument: the up-front order and its reason are now scoped. Finding resolved: the scope paragraph keeps only the bracket for the whole class (true for Ethereum-type designs and for designs such as Aptos, whose prologue checks before and epilogue applies after); the up-front charge and sequence-number advance are scoped to 'many designs within that scope, such as Ethereum'; the reason for charging first is scoped to 'these designs' (those that charge up front), with the reservation variant conditioned; a conditioned sentence covers designs that check sequence number and fee coverage before and charge and advance in a closing step; 'Either way' states only what holds for both (outside the undoable part). Settlement's 'never exceeds' and 'whole difference' are kept to designs that charged the full limit up front; the closing envelope sentence says 'charge'; flow title is Ethereum and its labels carry no conditions; model sequence and invariants fields match. Accuracy checked sentence by sentence: Ethereum's debit is gas limit times effective price; nonce advance sits outside the payload's snapshot (including creation); EIP-1559 burn/priority split for gas used; storage-clearing refunds lower the count; EIP-7702 delegations applied before and kept on failure; block-level steps before (system calls) and after (withdrawals); creation installs init code's output, which does not run; CREATE's contract nonce is a payload effect; non-refunding metered designs exist. Overlap: single placement under Transactions; no parent sentence restated except the carried-over post-state clause (advisory). Territory: Gas, Fees, Account Nonces, Metering, Fee Accounting, Logs, Events, State Roots, EVM, Contract Execution, Execution Context, Deterministic Execution, Transaction Validation, Transaction Atomicity and Transaction Reversion named, not explained; why the charge and number survive a revert left to Transaction Reversion; what is undone left to Transaction Atomicity; no lifecycle states. Structure: the designed process flow (bracket, three payload kinds converging, settlement, outputs) is written as designed; prose gives reasons and does not re-list stages. Canonical: no positional or time-sensitive words; American English. Depth follows the three claims; no repeated point after the repair dropped 'runs in full when the payload fails'. Advisory: (1) 'Either way' and the two-way contrast read as exhaustive, while hybrids exist (Starknet advances the nonce before execution and transfers the fee after); the conclusion still holds, and the model's sequence field carries the same two-way framing. (2) 'only check before the payload that the sender's sequence number is the expected one and that the payer can cover the maximum fee': 'only' contrasts with charging, but such prologues check more (expiry, chain identifier, authentication), and these checks are the validity checks at the position, which sits slightly awkwardly beside 'Execution starts from a transaction that met the validity rules'; 'check rather than apply' would be exact. (3) 'not always limited to these two': settlement is also a protocol step outside the payload; 'these two up-front effects' would be exact. (4) 'which is how each transaction comes to execute against what everything ordered before it left' closely paraphrases the parent's premise. (5) 'refund' in two senses: settlement refund and 'capped refunds for clearing storage' (a reduction of the counted usage). (6) The reservation variant is given without an example design; harmless as a conditional.

Contract Execution named in the closing paragraph to draw the unit boundary (one invocation of a contract's code); how an invocation enters, runs and ends is not explained.
Deterministic Execution named as owning committing to results so nodes detect divergence; no determinism argument in the record.
Events named with Logs as covering outputs that do not enter state; not explained.
EVM appears only as an example label ('the EVM's logs'); nothing about the machine is explained.
Execution Context named as owning what code can read; not explained.

Fee Accounting named as owning how the charge is divided and recorded; the record gives only Ethereum's burn/priority split as one example of distribution, within claim 1's 'distributing the fee as the protocol directs'.
Fees named with Gas as owning how resources are priced; 'fee' is used only for the charge the envelope applies; pricing and fee markets not explained.
Gas named as owning pricing; 'gas limit' and 'gas used' appear only as Ethereum's names for the declared limit and the usage; gas costs not explained.
Logs named ('which Logs and Events cover') as an output outside state that the record carries; not explained.

Metering named: exhausting the limit stops the payload 'by the rules of Metering'; the record says only that the settled usage is the metering count, which can differ from work performed (claim 1's 'resources actually used'); how metering counts is not explained.

Resource limits appear as the transaction's declared limit; the record uses only that the limit bounds consumption, which is the reason the worst case can be charged first; how limits are set or enforced is not explained.
State Roots named as owning how designs commit to states and records; not explained.
Transaction Atomicity named as owning what is undone and how; the record says only that the payload's transfer is undone with the payload's effects, a boundary between payload and fee.

Transaction Reversion named as owning why a reverted transaction keeps the charge and number and why some failures consume all remaining allowance; the record states where they sit, not why they survive; the record-needed argument is this concept's claim 2.

Transaction Validation named as deciding validity at the position; the pre-payload sequence-number and fee-coverage checks of Aptos-type designs are mentioned only as where those designs place the charge and update, within claim 1; how validation works is not explained.

model.meaning: The property that the state changes made by executing a transaction's payload, across every call it makes, take effect on the executing state machine together or not at all, with designs differing in what they keep outside that unit and in whether a caller can confine a callee's failure to the callee.

parents.transactions: Parent already says the transaction is the unit of atomicity (effects applied together or not at all) and that a transaction may revert past a bound; start beyond that, do not restate it. Adds: what exactly the unit covers (nested calls, which kinds of change) and what sits outside it; how execution environments implement it (journal vs buffered working copy, per-call checkpoints where needed); where designs narrow it to one call (handled callee failures) and what that does to the meaning of a success status; what it does not give (isolation from code the transaction calls) and where its scope ends (one transaction, one state machine).

claims: what the all-or-nothing unit covers inside one transaction: the state changes made by every call it makes, nested to any depth, including value transfers, storage writes, contracts created and, in designs such as the EVM, emitted logs; and what designs that keep a failed transaction's fee and sequence-number update place outside the unit, so that it is narrower than everything the transaction's processing changes. Why those survive a failure is Transaction Reversion's

how execution environments provide the unit on one state machine: recording each change in a journal so that it can be undone on failure, or buffering changes in a working copy that is applied only on success; the trade-off between them, such as cheap reads against the live state versus cheap discards; and why designs that let a caller continue after a callee fails need nested checkpoints, one per call, while designs in which any failure aborts the transaction need only one, so that a failure can be undone back to the point where the failing call began

where the unit is narrowed: in designs that let a caller handle a callee's failure, such as the EVM, a caller that handles it instead of propagating it keeps its own changes while the callee's are undone, so all-or-nothing holds per call, and the transaction as a whole is all-or-nothing only along paths where failures propagate; and why a successful status therefore does not show that every action the transaction attempted took effect. Contract Calls and Unchecked External Calls are named, not explained

what atomicity does not provide and where its scope ends: it does not hide a transaction's intermediate states from code the transaction itself calls, which can observe and act on them before the transaction finishes, so all-or-nothing is not isolation within a transaction; and it covers one transaction on one state machine, while all-or-nothing across several transactions, as with bundles, or across chains is provided, where it is, by other mechanisms. Reentrancy, Bundle Atomicity and Atomicity Guarantees are named, not explained

placements.transaction-atomicity: Single placement, under Transactions in Computation & Execution. Write for any transaction-executing state machine; mark design-specific facts with the design (EVM, Move-based chains, Solana, Cosmos SDK) rather than presenting EVM behavior as universal.

statement: Unit = the state changes made while executing the transaction's payload, across every call it makes however deep the nesting goes. Do not write 'unbounded depth': some designs bound call depth (the EVM at 1024 frames).

Kinds of change in the unit: value/balance transfers, storage writes, contracts created (the account and its installed code). Logs only with a design attached: in the EVM, logs of a failed frame are discarded with it; some designs keep diagnostic log output of failed transactions (Solana returns program logs for failed transactions), so do not write that logs are always undone. Plan wording 'where a design records them' is flagged as imprecise; condition it on the design, e.g. 'in designs such as the EVM'.

Outside the unit, in designs that include failed transactions (e.g. Ethereum, Solana): the fee charge, the sequence-number update where the design has one, and the record of the failure. So the unit is narrower than everything the transaction's processing changes. Name only that these survive; why they survive is Transaction Reversion's.

Scope: one transaction on one state machine. Not several transactions (bundles: Bundle Atomicity, name only), not across chains (Atomicity Guarantees, name only). Do not say such cross-transaction or cross-chain atomicity is impossible; say it is provided, where it is, by other mechanisms.
establishedBy: Journal (undo log): changes are written to the executing state as they happen, each recorded with what it replaced; a checkpoint is a position in the journal; on failure entries are undone in reverse order back to it. Many EVM clients work this way (e.g. go-ethereum's state journal, revm's journaled state). 'Live state' here means the in-memory state the execution reads, not the persisted database; clients also keep the block's changes in memory before committing them, so do not imply each write hits disk.

Buffered working copy (overlay, cache branch): writes go to a layer over the pre-state; on success the layer is merged into its parent (or the post-state); on failure it is dropped. Examples, hedged with 'for example': Cosmos SDK cache-wrapped stores, branched per transaction; Solana applies a transaction's account changes only if it succeeds, apart from the fee payer's charge.

Trade-off (the claim says 'such as', keep it hedged): journal = reads and commit are cheap, discarding costs work proportional to the changes undone; buffer = discarding is dropping a layer, but reads must look through the layers (cost grows with nesting unless flattened) and success needs a merge. Real clients can combine both; present two approaches, not a partition of every implementation, and never say a named client uses 'only' one.

Nested checkpoints: per-call checkpoints are needed only where a caller can continue after its callee fails (the EVM); there a journal position or a buffer layer per call lets the failing call's changes, including those of its already-successful descendants, be undone back to where it began. Where any failure aborts the whole transaction, one transaction-level checkpoint suffices. The plan claim's 'why either needs nested checkpoints, one per call' is flagged as an overclaim; write the condition.

Nesting consequence: a callee's success merges its changes into its caller's pending changes, not into final state; they are still undone if any ancestor frame fails. Only the top frame's success commits to the post-state.
confusions: All-or-nothing is not isolation: code the transaction calls (including a contract re-entered mid-call) reads the transaction's uncommitted writes and can act on them before the transaction ends. Reentrancy named only; no attack walkthrough. Between transactions, whether others see intermediate state is a matter of the execution model (sequential execution, or parallel designs that preserve a serial order): Sequential Execution and Parallel Execution are excluded, so at most name them, do not claim more.

A successful status is not proof every attempted action took effect: where callers may handle callee failures, the top frame can succeed after inner calls failed and were undone. Unchecked External Calls named only (a low-level call whose failure flag is ignored).
Atomic does not mean a failed transaction changes nothing: in designs that include failed transactions the fee, sequence-number update and failure record remain (point to Reversion for why).

Not the same as Bundle Atomicity, Atomicity Guarantees (cross-chain), Atomic Composability, or Atomic State Transitions (State & Data): name for boundary only, explain none. Do not drift into finality or reorganizations (an applied transaction can still be removed by a reorg); that is not in the claims.
invariants: Per call frame, on designs with catchable failures: when a frame ends, either all changes made in it and in its successfully completed descendants become part of its caller's pending changes, or none do. The transaction's payload changes reach the post-state only if the top frame succeeds.

Every node must undo exactly the same changes, or nodes diverge; undo is part of the consensus-critical execution rules, not a client choice. State this only if needed; do not explain Deterministic Execution.
variants: Catchable callee failure (the EVM): a failed call returns a failure indication to its caller, whose frame continues with its own earlier changes intact. The caller can propagate (revert in turn) or handle it. Solidity's high-level calls propagate by default; low-level calls return a status the code must check. Contract Calls named only; do not explain the call model.

Abort-whole-transaction (for example Move-based chains such as Aptos and Sui, where an abort ends the transaction and cannot be caught; Solana, where a failed cross-program invocation fails the transaction): the unit is not narrowed, and all-or-nothing holds for the transaction as a whole. Use 'for example' and do not claim these are the only such designs.

Wording pitfall for claim 3: 'all-or-nothing holds per call' applies to designs in the first variant; the plan claim states it without the platform condition (flagged). 'All-or-nothing only along paths where failures propagate' means: the whole transaction is all-or-nothing with respect to failures that propagate to the top frame; a handled failure leaves a partly effective transaction.
tradeoffs: Journal vs buffer: cheap reads and commits vs cheap discards (see establishedBy).

Catchable vs abort-all is a consequence to state, not a design argument to build: catchable failures let a caller recover or try an alternative but narrow the guarantee to one call and make an ignored failure a bug class; abort-all keeps the whole-transaction guarantee but gives the caller no recovery. Keep it to that; motives beyond the claims are out of scope.

design.relationship: A property defined by its boundary: what the unit covers and excludes, how it is enforced by nested checkpoints, where designs narrow it to one call, and one guarantee it is commonly mistaken for (isolation).

structures.purpose: Separate all-or-nothing (which effects land) from isolation (who can observe effects before the transaction ends): All-or-nothing ≠ Isolation.
structures.whyNotProse: Readers bring the database sense of a transaction, where atomicity and isolation arrive together, and read 'atomic' as 'invisible until done'. That specific conflation is the one this concept must undo, and marking it as a conflation names it as the reading to drop; the paragraph supplies why callees can see the transaction's uncommitted writes.

design.division: Prose carries every claim: the unit's coverage and what designs keep outside it, the journal and buffer approaches with their trade-off and when per-call checkpoints are needed, narrowing by handled failures and its effect on a success status, and the scope limit. The distinction only marks the two guarantees as different; the prose explains that code called by the transaction can observe and act on its intermediate state, and the distinction must not restate that reasoning.
design.level: The parent states only that the transaction's effects are applied together or not at all; how far that unit reaches into nested calls, how it is implemented, where it narrows and that it is not isolation are this concept's, at the leaf below Transactions. Cross-transaction and cross-chain atomicity belong to other concepts and are named only.
design.territory: Draws no sibling's relationship: Transaction Reversion owns triggers, what survives a failure and why, and revert data; this concept only places the fee, sequence-number update and record outside the unit. Transaction Execution owns the protocol envelope around the payload. Reentrancy, Contract Calls, Unchecked External Calls, Bundle Atomicity and Atomicity Guarantees are named, never explained. The distinction concerns atomicity's own scope, not reentrancy's mechanism.
design.placements: One placement, under Transactions; the design holds wherever the concept opens because it is stated per design (EVM, Move-based chains, Solana, Cosmos SDK) rather than as one machine's behavior.

Bundle Atomicity is named once ('as with bundles') to place multi-transaction all-or-nothing outside the scope; no bundle mechanism is explained. Unchanged by the repair.
