model.meaning: Note: the failure path of an included transaction whose execution fails: the effects its payload produced are discarded, and, in designs that include failed transactions, it stays in the chain recorded as failed, with the fee charged for the attempt and the protocol's own updates (such as the sequence-number update) kept. Scope is one transaction's failure on one state machine; not chain rollbacks or reorganizations (excluded), not validity (Validation).

parents.transactions: Premises not to re-teach: the all-or-nothing boundary; that reversion rolls back state changes while some systems still include the transaction with fees or nonce updates applied (domain text); that a transaction can carry bounds, such as a minimum acceptable price, beyond which it should revert. Adds: which triggers end execution and how they differ in cost; exactly what is discarded and what survives, and WHY each survivor survives; how the reason is reported and where it is (not) kept; reverting as a deliberate tool with its price and limits; the consequences that separate a reverted transaction from an invalid one.

claims: what triggers a revert and how the triggers differ in what the failure costs: an explicit revert by the running code, a failed check, running out of metered resources, or an invalid operation; and why, in the EVM for example, an explicit revert returns the unused part of the failing call's resource allowance while an exceptional halt consumes all of it, so the trigger decides how much of the failing call's allowance, and so of the sender's fee, a failure consumes. Gas and Metering are named, not explained

what reversion undoes and what survives it in designs that include failed transactions: state changes and emitted logs are discarded, while the fee charged for the attempt, the sequence-number update, in designs that use sequence numbers, and a record of the failure remain; and why each survives: an uncharged failure would let a sender impose execution work on every node at no cost, a sequence number left unspent would let the same signed transaction be executed again, and the record lets the sender and others see that it was included and failed

how a failure is reported and used: revert data returned to the caller, such as an error identifier with arguments, which a calling contract can decode, handle or pass upward, while in some designs, such as the EVM's receipts, it is not kept in the transaction's record, so an outside observer recovers the reason by re-executing the transaction; and reverting as an enforcement tool, code that checks a condition such as an access right or a minimum acceptable result and reverts when it fails, so effects that depended on it never land where the failure propagates, at the price of the fee for the attempt and with protection only for the conditions the code checks

the difference between an invalid transaction and a reverted one in their consequences: in designs that validate blocks by executing them, an invalid transaction cannot be included, so it leaves no record, costs its sender nothing and leaves its sequence number free, while a reverted one is included, recorded as failed, charged and consumes its sequence number; and why designs that make every condition a validity rule, as Bitcoin does with its scripts, have no reverted outcome at all, since a failing condition makes the transaction invalid. Transaction Validation owns where the line between the two is drawn

placements.transaction-reversion: Single L2 placement (Computation & Execution / Transactions / Transaction Reversion), leaf. Stand without the parent: say once what 'reverted' means (included, executed, failed) before building on it. Every EVM-specific statement carries 'in the EVM' or 'such as'; general statements are scoped to 'designs that include failed transactions' or 'designs that validate blocks by executing them'.

sequence: Transaction-level path only (message-calls owns how a callee's failure is reported inside a call; atomicity owns how changes are undone and the per-call narrowing): execution hits a trigger, the failing frame's changes are discarded, the failure propagates to the top (or is handled by a caller: name atomicity, do not explain), the transaction ends with a failed outcome, the fee charged for the attempt and, in designs that use sequence numbers, the sequence-number update stand, a failure record is kept.
The charge and sequence-number update are applied outside the payload before it runs (transaction-execution's ordering, name only); reversion's angle is why they are kept, not when they are applied.
actors: Running code: reverts explicitly when its own condition fails.
The execution environment: halts exceptionally (out of metered resources, invalid operation).
Calling contract: receives revert data; decodes, handles or passes it upward (name only at that depth: message-calls owns the call-level report).
Sender: pays for the failed attempt; learns the outcome from the record.
Outside observers (wallets, explorers, indexers): see inclusion and failure from the record; recover the reason by re-executing.
inputs: Triggers. Two cost classes in the EVM: explicit revert (REVERT opcode; leftover allowance of the failing call returned to its caller, and at top level the unused part is not charged) vs exceptional halt (out of gas, invalid opcode, and other invalid operations such as a bad jump or a state change in a read-only context; the failing call's whole allowance is consumed).

Pitfall: the four named triggers are not four cost classes. 'Failed check' is not its own class: a check in the code usually ends in an explicit revert (Solidity's require and custom errors, and since Solidity 0.8 also assert and arithmetic panics), while older compilers' assert used an invalid opcode and so consumed everything. Running out of resources is itself an exceptional halt. Cost follows the halt type, not the reason.

Pitfall: 'consumes all of it' applies to the failing call's allowance. That equals the sender's whole declared limit only when the top-level call halts; a nested call is given at most part of the caller's remaining allowance (in the EVM, all but one 64th). Do not say an exceptional halt always charges the full limit. Avoid 'burn' for this: fee burning is a different thing (transaction-execution names it).
Explicit revert still charges for everything executed up to the revert.
outputs: Discarded: the payload's state changes (storage writes, value transfers, contracts created) and the logs it emitted, in designs such as the EVM where logs are part of the reverted effects.

Kept, in designs that include failed transactions: the fee charged for the attempt (in designs that charge by usage, such as Ethereum, the charge for the resources consumed; not every design charges by consumption, e.g. Solana and Cosmos SDK chains by default); the sequence-number update in designs that use sequence numbers (designs without them keep the equivalent mark of use, e.g. Solana records the transaction's signature and rejects a repeat while the transaction's recent blockhash is still accepted); a record of the outcome with failed status. Do not say these are the only survivors: some formats apply other effects outside the payload that also stand (e.g. EIP-7702 delegations set before execution).
Why the charge stays: every validating node re-executes the transaction; an uncharged failure would let anyone impose that work for free. Denial-of-Service Resistance named, not explained.

Why the sequence-number update stays: otherwise the same signed transaction stays valid and anyone holding it could have it included and executed again, charging the sender again each time. Replay Protection and Account Nonces named, not explained.

Why the record stays: the transaction was included and consumed the sender's fee and sequence number; the sender and readers of the chain need to see that it was included and failed, not that it is still pending or was dropped. Record contents are transaction-execution's (name).

Revert data: bytes returned by an explicit revert, commonly an error identifier with encoded arguments (Solidity: 4-byte selector plus arguments; standard Error(string) and Panic(code)). Exceptional halts return no data. EVM receipts keep status, resources used and logs, not revert data; recovering the reason needs re-execution against the pre-state at the transaction's position (a node with that historical state or a tracing facility). Re-execution after the fact is not Transaction Simulation (prediction before submission; excluded, name only).
assumptions: Survivors claim holds in designs that include failed transactions (Ethereum and EVM chains, Solana, Cosmos SDK chains in their way); not in designs where every condition is a validity rule (Bitcoin).

Invalid-vs-reverted consequences ('no record, costs nothing, sequence number free') hold in designs that validate blocks by executing them. In designs that order transactions without executing them (some rollups), an invalid transaction can sit in the ordered data and be skipped by every node: Validation's claim, name only, keep the condition.

Do not generalize Bitcoin to all UTXO designs: Cardano validates scripts in a second phase and includes a transaction whose scripts fail, forfeiting its collateral instead of applying it; a reverted-like outcome exists there. Use only if needed; otherwise keep 'as Bitcoin does'.
failures: Enforcement limits: a revert protects only the conditions the code checks. A minimum acceptable result still admits every outcome at or above the bound; a missing or wrong check protects nothing. The sender pays for every failed attempt.

'Effects that depended on the check never land' holds for the reverting call and every caller that propagates the failure; a caller that handles it keeps its own effects (Transaction Atomicity owns this narrowing; name it, do not explain). Do not state the enforcement guarantee unconditionally.
Reverted is not harmless: a sender can lose most or all of the allowance (exceptional halt at top level) for no effect.
variants: Designs that include failed transactions (reverted outcome exists: included, charged, sequence consumed, recorded failed) vs designs that make every condition a validity rule (Bitcoin scripts: failing makes the transaction invalid; no reverted outcome, no charge for failure). Where the line is drawn and why is Transaction Validation's; reversion states only the consequences of each outcome.
Explicit revert vs exceptional halt (EVM): what is returned (leftover allowance, revert data) vs consumed (whole allowance of the failing call, no data).
invariants: A reverted transaction in an execution-validated design with sequence numbers leaves on the chain: the fee charged for the attempt, its sequence number used, a failed record, and any other effects the format applies outside the payload; none of the failed payload's state changes or logs. Where a caller handled a nested failure, the undo is per call path (atomicity's narrowing, name only).
tradeoffs: Including failures (charge the sender, keep nodes paid for their work, let contracts enforce arbitrary conditions) vs making every condition a validity rule (failures cost nothing to the sender but conditions must stay cheap to decide, so arbitrary checks are not possible as validity rules). State as consequence only; the reasoning about the line's placement is Validation's.

design.relationship: A failure path with conditions (what triggers it, what it costs, what is discarded and what survives and why, how the reason is reported and used) plus one real conflation: invalid and reverted transactions are both called failed, yet differ in every consequence (included or not, recorded or not, charged or not, sequence number used or free).

structures.purpose: Mark the conflation 'Invalid transaction ≠ Reverted transaction' at the point where the record turns to consequences, so that a reader who calls both 'failed' sees they are different outcomes before reading what each means.
structures.whyNotProse: Prose carries the consequences and their conditions, but the two outcomes share the everyday word 'failed' and the confusion is the one users and tooling make (a reverted transaction shown as failed is assumed to have cost nothing). A distinction marks that non-identity as a claim of its own; inside a paragraph it reads as one more contrast among many.

design.division: Prose explains the triggers and their cost classes, what is discarded and why each survivor survives, reporting and enforcement, and the consequences of each outcome with their design conditions (block validation by execution; Bitcoin's validity-only conditions). The distinction shows only that the two are different outcomes; the prose must not restate it as a slogan, and the distinction must not carry the consequences or conditions.
design.level: The parent states the boundary and, as a premise, that some systems keep fees or nonce updates after a revert; the triggers, their costs, the reasons each survivor survives, reporting and the invalid-versus-reverted consequences are this concept's. The distinction belongs here, not at Validation: Validation owns where the line is drawn, reversion owns what each outcome means.
design.territory: Names, never explains: Gas and Metering (cost units), Fees and Fee Accounting (charge, settlement), Account Nonces and Replay Protection (why reuse is prevented generally), Transaction Execution (when the charge and sequence update are applied; record contents), Transaction Atomicity (how changes are undone; per-call narrowing when a caller handles a failure), Message Calls and Contract Calls (call-level failure report), Transaction Validation (where the invalid/reverted line is drawn), Transaction Simulation, Denial-of-Service Resistance, Logs and Events, Rollbacks and Reorganizations (chain-level undo, not this). Atomicity's distinction (all-or-nothing vs isolation) is a different pair. The parent's bound example (minimum acceptable price) is a premise: build on it with price and limits, do not restate it.
